sections.html:
Arkansas doesn't have one anymore. Act 645 of 2003 ended it, and anyone who died after December 31, 2004 leaves behind no state estate tax return.

That answers the first question most heirs ask. Arkansas takes no cut of the estate because of its size, and there is no state form to prepare for it. The Department of Finance and Administration publishes a one-page notice about the repeal. Print it for the probate file in case a title company or lender wants proof.

The notice speaks only to the estate tax. If the inheritance is large, run the details past a probate attorney before you distribute anything.

The federal tax applies to a small slice of estates. A return is due only if the gross estate, added to adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, tops the filing threshold for the year of death. For a 2026 death that threshold is $15,000,000.

Plain, modest estates seldom need to file. When one does, the gross estate is counted at its fair market value on the date of death. Deductions can include mortgages and other debts, administration expenses, anything passing to a surviving spouse and gifts to qualified charities. A surviving spouse can also elect portability on a timely filed return, which carries over the decedent's unused exemption.

sections.h2: Income tax when an heir sells
sections.html:
Usually the bill is small, because an heir's tax basis starts at the home's worth on the day the owner died. Under Publication 551, that date-of-death market value is the basis, unless the personal representative elects the alternate valuation date. An heir who gets a Schedule A (Form 8971) generally works from the estate tax value shown on it.

The taxable gain is the distance between that starting number and the sale price. Sell close to the date-of-death value and the gain stays modest. Wait while the market climbs and the increase becomes the gain. Arkansas taxes half of a net long-term gain.

Rent or other income the estate collects before closing is a different topic. The state tax agency has a page of fiduciary and estate income tax forms that personal representatives can use.

Smaller estates can skip a personal representative. Ark. Code 28-41-101 lets a distributee collect and pass along the assets when property owned at death, less encumbrances, is no more than $100,000. A surviving spouse's or minor children's statutory allowances and the decedent's homestead are left out of the count.

The homestead carve-out is the part that matters with real estate. A family home that was the homestead doesn't eat into the $100,000, although it still gets listed in the affidavit.

  • Wait at least 45 days from the date of death.
  • Make sure no petition to appoint a personal representative is pending or granted.
  • File an affidavit, signed by one or more distributees, with the probate clerk of the circuit court in the proper county.
  • State in it that no claims remain unpaid and that the Department of Human Services either furnished no benefits or was reimbursed.
  • List personal property with values, plus real property by legal description and value, homestead included.
  • Pay the clerk $25 to file and $5 per certified copy. Attaching a will adds no fee.

sections.h2: When the estate holds real property
sections.html:
Thirty days after filing is the deadline for publishing a notice of the death along with the affidavit. From the first publication, creditors have three months to present verified claims, and any that arrive late are barred.

Build your selling timeline around those three months. Buyers and title companies often want to see the filed affidavit, the published notice and a closed claims period before they will accept a deed. The distributee can also open a bank account in the estate's name with no petition or court order, handy for sale proceeds and last bills.

An estate over the limit, or one where heirs disagree, goes to regular administration in the circuit court's probate division. That path has different filings, so ask a probate attorney which applies.

The state's main closing charge is the real property transfer tax, $3.30 per $1,000 of actual consideration on a deed or instrument conveying realty, for transactions over $100. Ark. Code 26-60-105 breaks that into $1.10 per $1,000 plus a further $2.20 per $1,000 that the purchaser pays.

The county collector takes property tax from the first business day of March through October 15 (Ark. Code 26-36-201). After October 15 the bill is delinquent and a 10% penalty applies. If the estate is still being settled in the fall, check that the current bill hasn't slipped by.

Utilities, insurance and upkeep keep running until the deed is recorded. An empty inherited house can therefore cost money every month even though the estate owes no tax.

Sort out who legally owns the house and what paperwork is due, and only then choose between keeping, renting and selling.

  • Find the will, the deed and the newest property tax statement.
  • Call the county assessor or collector about the parcel's tax status.
  • Decide whether the small estate affidavit fits or a personal representative is needed.
  • Get a date-of-death value in writing. It sets the basis for a later sale.
  • Lock the house and keep the insurance active.
  • Talk to a probate attorney and a tax professional before signing a contract.

A short timeline helps. In the first weeks, secure the house and gather papers. At the 45-day mark, a small estate can file its affidavit. Publication follows within 30 days, and then the three-month creditor window runs. Only after that is a clean sale usually possible, unless a personal representative is appointed and handles it another way.

Heirs who live out of state, or who inherited a house needing repairs, sometimes sell for cash to stop the carrying costs and skip the repair projects. A cash buyer closes as-is, and the title company will confirm the estate's papers before the closing date. Ask the title company early what it will need from the estate. Which route suits you depends on the documents and on how soon the family wants this settled.

faqs.q: Is there an Arkansas estate tax?
faqs.a: No. Act 645 of 2003 ended it, and no estate tax return is required for decedents who died after December 31, 2004.

faqs.q: Do heirs owe tax on income the estate earns before the house sells?
faqs.a: That falls outside the estate tax. The Department of Finance and Administration keeps a page of fiduciary and estate income tax forms for personal representatives.

faqs.q: At what size does the federal estate tax apply?
faqs.a: A return is due only if the gross estate, with adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption, tops the filing threshold for the year of death. For 2026 that threshold is $15,000,000.

faqs.q: What is the Arkansas small estate limit?
faqs.a: Property owned at death can total up to $100,000 after encumbrances, not counting the homestead and statutory allowances for a surviving spouse or minor children. Wait at least 45 days after death, and expect a three-month creditor window after the notice is first published.

faqs.q: Will I owe tax if I sell an inherited house right away?
faqs.a: Usually little. Your basis is the date-of-death fair market value, so the gain is the sale price minus that figure, and Arkansas taxes half of a net long-term gain.
